t: Prime Palindrome — Generate Palindromes, Test Primality
o:
We need the smallest number ≥ n that is simultaneously a prime and a palindrome. Checking numbers one by one seems natural, but palindromic primes are extremely sparse: after 13 there are no 2-digit ones, and every even-length palindrome is divisible by 11, so none of those can be prime. The gap between consecutive prime palindromes near 10^8 can be huge (e.g. from 98689 to 1003001), so a linear scan that tests every integer is far too slow. The key structural fact: any palindrome is fully determined by its left half, so we can enumerate candidates by generating palindromes directly instead of scanning all integers. Since answers fit under 2·10^8, we only ever need palindromes up to 9 digits, i.e. roots up to ~10^5.

**Examples.** n = 6: 6 is not prime, 7 is prime and a palindrome → 7. n = 8: 8, 9, 10 fail; 11 is prime and palindromic → 11. n = 13: 13 is prime but not a palindrome; 14–99 contain no prime palindromes (even-length palindromes like 22, 33 are multiples of 11); 101 is the next candidate → 101.
k: Every even-length palindrome is divisible by 11, so only odd-length palindromes need to be considered.
A palindrome is determined by its first half (the root), so enumerate roots 1..10^5 and build odd-length palindromes in increasing order.
Trial division up to sqrt(x) suffices for primality since x ≤ 2·10^8 means at most ~14142 divisions per test.

a.i: Start at n and walk upward, returning the first number that passes both a palindrome check and a trial-division primality check. This is the most direct translation of the problem statement. It is correct but slow because prime palindromes are sparse — the scan may cross millions of non-candidates between hits.
s: Check if x reads the same reversed; if not, continue.
Check primality by trial division against all integers from 2 to floor(sqrt(x)).
Return x as soon as both checks pass.
a.t: Worst case roughly O(D · sqrt(M)) where D is the size of the gap to the next prime palindrome and M ≤ 2·10^8 — the palindrome filter prunes most numbers, but large gaps make this too slow in practice.
a.sp: O(1) — only a few scalar variables.

a.n: Approach 2: Generate Odd-Length Palindromes from Roots
a.i: Instead of testing every integer, generate palindromes directly in increasing order of length. For each root r, mirror all but the last digit to form an odd-length palindrome (e.g. root 123 → 12321). Even-length palindromes are skipped entirely since they are divisible by 11 and hence composite (except 11 itself, handled specially). For each generated palindrome ≥ n, run trial division; the first prime found is the answer. Because roots go up to only 10^5 and each yields one candidate, this is fast enough with ease.
s: Handle small cases: if n ≤ 2 return 2, and if 8 ≤ n ≤ 11 return 11 (covers the even-length exception).
Build the odd-length palindrome by appending the reverse of r without its last digit (e.g. r=12 → 121).
If the palindrome is ≥ n and passes trial division up to its square root, return it.
The loop terminates well before r exceeds 10^5 because an answer exists below 2·10^8.
a.t: O(sqrt(N) · log N) overall — about 10^5 roots, each palindrome tested with O(sqrt(p)) ≈ 1.4·10^4 divisions worst case, which runs comfortably fast.
a.sp: O(log N) — string storage for building each palindrome.

w: In an interview, mention the brute-force idea briefly, then pivot to generating palindromes from their halves — that is the expected solution. Critical pitfalls: forgetting that 11 is the only prime palindrome with an even digit count (it must be special-cased or you will miss answers like n = 8), using 32-bit overflow-prone arithmetic when mirroring near 10^8 (use 64-bit in C++/Java), and checking primality before palindromicity in the brute force (palindrome check is cheaper, so order matters). Edge cases: n = 1 → 2, n = 2 → 2, n = 8 → 11, n = 13 → 101. Likely follow-ups: prove why even-length palindromes are divisible by 11 (alternating digit sum vanishes), or extend to finding all prime palindromes in a range using a sieve over generated candidates.
